name: Spain
governanceModel: First EU member with a dedicated national AI supervisory agency
debateTopics: Organic Law's sanctions regime passing the Cortes intact
overview:
Spain was the first EU member state to stand up a dedicated national AI authority — AESIA, the Spanish AI Supervisory Agency, headquartered in A Coruña and operational since June 2024. In May 2026 the Council of Ministers approved a draft Organic Law on AI governance that would formally adapt the EU AI Act into Spanish national law and establish an AESIA-managed regulatory sandbox; some analyses indicate it would also repeal the prior 2023 sandbox decree, though that specific detail was not independently confirmed in this review. As of this writing the law remains before the Cortes, not yet passed.

Minister for Digital Transformation and Civil Service Óscar López has taken a notably measured public tone, cautioning that 'nobody should overreact' against the EU AI Act — a contrast with some peer states' more assertive national add-on legislation.

Some analyses report it would also repeal the prior 2023 sandbox decree, though that detail was not independently confirmed. researchEcosystem.summary: Spanish AI research spans the Technical University of Madrid, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, the University of the Basque Country, and CSIC/BIST/ICREA. Seedtable, an industry listicle rather than a primary data source, estimates this ecosystem has produced over 360 VC-backed spinouts with a combined value of roughly $10.5B — a figure that has not been independently verified.

debates.summary: As the first EU state with a dedicated AI authority, Spain's approach to sandbox design and enforcement is being cited by some analysts as an early reference point — positive or cautionary — for other member states.
debates.expanded: AESIA's regulatory sandbox lets companies trial AI systems under supervision before full compliance is required. How strictly AESIA moves from sandbox permissiveness to full enforcement once the Organic Law passes could influence whether other member states come to view Spain's early-mover approach as a template worth following.

debates.topic: Organic Law's sanctions regime passing the Cortes intact
debates.summary: The draft Organic Law's sanctions and enforcement provisions still need to survive parliamentary negotiation before becoming binding.
debates.expanded: Council of Ministers approval is only the first step — Spain's minority-coalition politics mean the sanctions regime and sandbox provisions could still be amended before the law passes the Cortes, and Minister López's measured public tone suggests the government may be open to softening some provisions during negotiation.
